title: The Raft of the Medusa

slides.headline: 147 people on a raft. Only 15 were found alive.
slides.sub: Théodore Géricault, The Raft of the Medusa, 1818-1819

slides.headline: A true story
slides.text: In 1816 the French frigate Méduse ran aground off the coast of West Africa. There weren't enough lifeboats, so about 150 people were put on a makeshift raft.

slides.headline: Cut loose
slides.text: The lifeboats were supposed to tow the raft. Instead, the ropes were let go. The people on board drifted for 13 days with almost no food or water.

slides.headline: A father and his son
slides.text: Bottom left, an old man holds the body of a young man. He doesn't look for rescue. He has already lost everything.

slides.headline: The dead in the foreground
slides.text: Géricault studied real bodies in hospitals to paint them. On the raft, people fought, died, and some survivors resorted to cannibalism.

slides.headline: Do you see the ship?
slides.text: A tiny dot on the horizon: the Argus, the ship that would rescue them. Everyone on the raft is straining towards it.

slides.headline: Hope, at the top
slides.text: The bodies form a pyramid that rises from despair at the bottom to a man waving a cloth at the very top.

slides.headline: Bigger than life
slides.text: The canvas is about 5 by 7 metres, so the figures in front are larger than real people. You don't look at the raft, you stand on it.

slides.headline: A scandal
slides.text: The disaster was blamed on an inexperienced captain who got the job through political connections. The painting turned a cover-up into a national scandal.
